hook_text: In 1935, the sky over America went black in the middle of the day, and the darkness was made of farms.
clip_script: Picture endless grassland, with roots deep in the soil. Then come the tractors. Millions of hectares are ploughed up for wheat. Then the rain stops. The wheat dies. The bare soil turns to powder. And the wind arrives. Giant clouds of dust roll across the land, so thick that day becomes night. They called them black blizzards. The worst came on 14 April 1935, Black Sunday. Families lost everything. The lesson was clear: take away the plants that hold the soil, and the wind will take the soil. Today, farmers fight back. They plough across slopes, not down them. They build terraces. They leave old crop stalks to cover the ground. They plant trees to break the wind. Farming can destroy soil, or it can save it.
visual_style: Old black-and-white photographs of a towering dust cloud over a farm; a tractor ploughing prairie; cracked dry fields; a fence half-buried in dust; modern contour-ploughed fields seen from above; terraced hillsides; a no-till planter sowing into crop residue.
pacing: Building tension to the dust storm, then calmer and practical.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to see how farming causes soil erosion and how farmers can stop it.
